question.text: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=-2.$ Given that the point $P(-2,0,8)$ lies on $C$, and that $f_y = x\cos y + 4y + x$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
question.explanation:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z = f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=-2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(-2,0,8)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\dfrac {\partial z} {\partial y} \Bigg|_{(-2,0)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\dfrac {\partial z} {\partial y}$ at $(-2,0)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial z} {\partial y}\Bigg |_{(-2,0)} &=(-2)\cos 0 + 4(0) + (-2)\\[3pt] &= -2 - 2\\[3pt] &= -4 \end{align*}

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

\begin{align*} z - z|_{(-2,0)} &= \dfrac {\partial z} {\partial y}\Bigg |_{(-2,0)}(y-0) \\[5pt] z - 8 &= -4(y-0) \\[5pt] z &= -4y+8 \end{align*}

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(-2,0,8)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows: \[ \begin{cases} x = -2 \\[3pt] z = -4y+8 \end{cases} \]

question.text: A surface $S$ is defined by $z=f(x,y).$ The curve $C$ is the intersection of $S$ with the plane $x=1.$ Given that the point $P(1,1,-1)$ lies on $C$, and that $f_y = \dfrac{e^x-e^y}{2x}+2y$, find the slope of the tangent to $C$ at $P.$
question.explanation:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P(1,1,-1)$ will be given by the partial derivative $f_y(1,1).$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $f_y(x,y)$ at $(1,1)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} f_y(1,1) &= \dfrac{e^1-e^1}{2(1)}+2(1) \\[5pt] &= 0+2 \\[3pt] &=2 \end{align*}

question.text: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=-\dfrac{\pi}{2}.$ Given that the point $P\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2},0,2\right)$ lies on $C$, and that $f_y =\dfrac{\sin x\cos y}{2}$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
question.explanation:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=-\dfrac{\pi}{2}.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative $f_y\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2},0\right).$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $f_y(x,y)$ at $\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2},0\right)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} f_y\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2},0\right) &= \dfrac{\sin\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\cos 0}{2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{(-1)\cdot 1}{2} \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac 1 2 \end{align*}

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

\begin{align*} z - f\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2},0\right) &= f_y\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2},0\right)\left(y-0\right) \\[3pt] z - 2&= -\dfrac 1 2 y \\[3pt] z &= -\dfrac{1}{2} y +2 \end{align*}

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2},0,2\right)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes: \[ \begin{cases} x = -\dfrac{\pi}{2} \\ z = -\dfrac 1 2 y + 2 \end{cases} \]

Next, notice that:

  • For the plane $x = -\dfrac{\pi}{2},$ a normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n}_1 = \langle 1,0,0 \rangle.$

  • For the plane $z = -\dfrac 1 2 y + 2$ (or $y+2z-4=0$), a normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n}_2 = \langle 0,1,2 \rangle.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{n}_1 \times \mathbf{n}_2 & = \langle 1, 0, 0 \rangle \times \langle 0, 1, 2 \rangle \\[5pt] &= \begin{array}{|ccc|} \mathbf i & \mathbf j & \mathbf k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \end{array} \\[5pt] &=-2\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k} \\[5pt] &= \langle 0,-2,1\rangle \end{align*}

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $\langle 0,-2,1\rangle.$

question.text: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=-2.$ Given that the point $P(4,-2,5)$ lies on $C$, and that $f_x = y\sqrt{x}$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
question.explanation:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z = f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=-2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(4,-2,5)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\dfrac {\partial z} {\partial x} \Bigg|_{(4,-2)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\dfrac {\partial z} {\partial x}$ at $(4,-2)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial z} {\partial x}\Bigg |_{(4,-2)} &=(-2)\sqrt{4} \\[5pt] &= - 2(2) \\[5pt] &= -4 \end{align*}

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

\begin{align*} z - z|_{(4,-2)} &= \dfrac {\partial z} {\partial x}\Bigg |_{(4,-2)}(x-4) \\[5pt] z - 5 &= -4(x-4) \\[5pt] z &= -4x+21 \end{align*}

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(4,-2,5)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows: \[ \begin{cases} y = -2 \\[5pt] z =-4x+21 \end{cases} \]

question.text: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=1.$ Given that the point $P(1,0,-1)$ lies on $C$, and that $f_y = xe^{xy}-2\cos y$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
question.explanation:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative $f_y(1,0).$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $f_y(x,y)$ at $(1,0)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} f_y(1,0) &= 1\cdot e^{1\cdot 0}-2\cos 0 \\[5pt] &= 1\cdot 1-2\cdot 1\\[5pt] &= -1 \end{align*}

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

\begin{align*} z - f(1,0) &= f_y(1,0)(y-0) \\[5pt] z - (-1) &= (-1)y \\[5pt] z &= -y - 1 \end{align*}

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,0,-1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes: \[ \begin{cases} x = 1 \\ z = -y - 1 \end{cases} \]

Next, notice that:

  • For the plane $x = 1,$ a normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n}_1 = \langle 1,0,0 \rangle.$

  • For the plane $z = -y - 1$ (or $y+z+1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n}_2 = \langle 0,1,1 \rangle.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{n}_1 \times \mathbf{n}_2 & = \langle 1, 0, 0 \rangle \times \langle 0, 1, 1 \rangle \\[5pt] &= \begin{array}{|ccc|} \mathbf i & \mathbf j & \mathbf k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{array} \\[5pt] &=-\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k} \end{align*}

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $-\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}.$
